intro: These endings sit on a verb stem, a verb form or a noun and colour it in one of five ways: how often or how much a tendency shows (がち, 気味, っぽい, だらけ), which phase an action has reached (きる, かけ, っぱなし, ぬく), which way a change is heading (一方だ, つつある, ばかりだ), why you cannot avoid an action (ざるを得ない, ないわけにはいかない, ずにはいられない), and whether something can or might happen (かねない, かねる, 得る, がたい). In each set, ask the one question that separates the members, then check the form the ending attaches to: stem, dictionary form or ない-form.

skills.rule: がち = tends to happen often (unwelcome); 気味 = slightly, a touch of (a state now); っぽい = -ish, like, easily does (casual); だらけ = covered in, full of (too much).
skills.explain:
がち attaches to a verb stem or a noun and says something happens often, usually something you would rather avoid: 忘れがち 'apt to forget', 遅れがち 'often late', 病気がち 'often ill', 曇りがち 'mostly cloudy'. It behaves like a na-adjective: 遅れがちな電車.

気味 (ぎみ) also follows a stem or noun, but measures degree, not frequency: a slight dose of a state you feel now. 風邪気味 'a bit of a cold', 疲れ気味 'a bit tired', 太り気味 'a bit overweight'.

っぽい is casual and turns a noun, stem or i-adjective stem into an i-adjective: 子供っぽい 'childish', 白っぽい 'whitish', 安っぽい 'cheap-looking', 怒りっぽい 'quick to anger'. With verbs it names a personality trait: 忘れっぽい 'forgetful'.

だらけ takes nouns only and means a surface or a thing is full of something, too much and unpleasant: 泥だらけ 'covered in mud', 間違いだらけ 'riddled with mistakes'. Not for good things: 'full of flowers' is 花でいっぱい.
patterns: [verb stem / noun] がち (だ / な / の)
[verb stem / noun] 気味 (だ / の)
[noun / verb stem / i-adj stem] っぽい
[noun] だらけ (だ / の / になる)

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は少[すこ]し風邪[かぜ]{気味[ぎみ]}です。
examples.en: I have a bit of a cold today.

examples.jp: 冬[ふゆ]は運動不足[うんどうぶそく]になり{がち}だ。
examples.en: In winter people tend to get too little exercise.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]には子供[こども]{っぽい}ところがある。
examples.en: He has a childish side.

examples.jp: 雨[あめ]の中[なか]を歩[ある]いて、靴[くつ]が泥[どろ]{だらけ}になった。
examples.en: I walked in the rain and my shoes got covered in mud.

examples.jp: この作文[さくぶん]は間違[まちが]い{だらけ}です。
examples.en: This essay is full of mistakes.

examples.jp: 最近[さいきん]、約束[やくそく]を忘[わす]れ{がち}で困[こま]っている。
examples.en: Lately I keep forgetting appointments, and it's a problem.

contrast.note: がち counts how often: 遅れがち 'often late'. 気味 measures how much, now: 遅れ気味 'running a little behind'.
Casual and descriptive: 'looks like, has the feel of'. 忘れっぽい describes a forgetful person; 忘れがち says forgetting keeps happening.
でいっぱい is neutral 'full of'; だらけ is always too much and unpleasant.

mistakes.bad: 今日[きょう]は少[すこ]し風邪[かぜ]{がち}です。
mistakes.good: 今日[きょう]は少[すこ]し風邪[かぜ]{気味[ぎみ]}です。
mistakes.note: A slight state you have right now is 気味; がち would claim it happens often.

mistakes.bad: 庭[にわ]は花[はな]{だらけ}できれいだ。
mistakes.good: 庭[にわ]は花[はな]{でいっぱい}できれいだ。
mistakes.note: だらけ is for unwanted excess; a garden full of lovely flowers is でいっぱい.

skills.tip: How often? がち. How much, right now? 気味. Looks like what? っぽい. How much stuff on it? だらけ.

skills.rule: Stem + きる = do all of it, to the end; かけ = started and left half-done; っぱなし = left in that state (carelessly) or nonstop; ぬく = carry through to the end against difficulty.
skills.explain:
All four follow the verb stem and place the action on a line from start to finish.

きる means nothing is left: 読み切る 'read to the end', 使い切る 'use up', 疲れ切る 'be utterly exhausted'. Its potential negative is very common: 食べきれない 'can't eat it all'.

かけ is the opposite: begun, then stopped. As a noun with の: 読みかけの本 'a half-read book', 食べかけのパン. As a verb, かける: 言いかけてやめた 'started to say something and stopped'.

っぱなし says a state has been left as it is, usually through neglect: 電気をつけっぱなし 'leave the light on', 窓を開けっぱなし. It also means 'nonstop' for tiring states: 立ちっぱなし 'standing the whole time'.

ぬく adds will power: 走り抜く 'run the whole race', やり抜く 'see it through', 守り抜く 'protect to the last'. Where きる counts what is finished, ぬく praises the effort; 最後まで走りきった and 走り抜いた can both be right.
patterns: [verb stem] きる / きれない
[verb stem] かけの [noun] / かけて
[verb stem] っぱなし (にする / で)

examples.jp: こんなにたくさんは食[た]べ{きれない}。
examples.en: I can't eat all of this.

examples.jp: 一晩[ひとばん]でこの本[ほん]を読[よ]み{きった}。
examples.en: I read this whole book in one night.

examples.jp: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に読[よ]み{かけ}の雑誌[ざっし]がある。
examples.en: There's a half-read magazine on the desk.

examples.jp: 窓[まど]を開[あ]け{っぱなし}で出[で]かけてしまった。
examples.en: I went out and left the window open.

examples.jp: 一日中[いちにちじゅう]立[た]ち{っぱなし}で、足[あし]が痛[いた]い。
examples.en: I've been on my feet all day and my legs hurt.

examples.jp: 彼女[かのじょ]は最後[さいご]まで戦[たたか]い{ぬいた}。
examples.en: She fought it through to the very end.

contrast.note: The opposite of きる: 読みきった 'finished reading', 読みかけ 'half-read'.
ておく leaves something on purpose for later; っぱなし leaves it through carelessness.
ぬく stresses perseverance against hardship; きる simply means nothing is left undone.

mistakes.bad: 食[た]べ{きった}パンがまだ残[のこ]っている。
mistakes.good: 食[た]べ{かけ}のパンがまだ残[のこ]っている。
mistakes.note: Bread that is still there was not eaten up; half-eaten is かけ.

mistakes.bad: 明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]のために、資料[しりょう]を出[だ]し{っぱなし}にした。
mistakes.good: 明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]のために、資料[しりょう]を出[だ]し{ておいた}。
mistakes.note: Putting things out on purpose for later is ておく; っぱなし means you never put them away.

skills.tip: Is anything left? None: きる. Half: かけ. Never put back: っぱなし. Finished through grit: ぬく.

skills.rule: Dictionary form + 一方だ / ばかりだ = the change keeps going one way (ばかりだ: almost always for the worse); stem + つつある = the change is under way now.
skills.explain:
In this sense all three need a verb of change: 増える, 減る, 上がる, 悪くなる, 広がる, 変わる. つつある and 一方だ never work with a plain activity such as 食べる. With an activity verb, dictionary form + ばかりだ means something else: 'does nothing but' (泣くばかりだ).

一方だ follows the dictionary form and says a trend only goes one direction and nothing stops it: 人口は減る一方だ 'the population just keeps falling'. It is usually negative but can be neutral (客は増える一方だ).

ばかりだ has the same shape and meaning but is almost always for things getting worse, with a note of frustration: 病気は悪くなるばかりだ. Do not confuse it with た-form + ばかりだ 'have just done': 食べたばかりだ.

つつある follows the stem and belongs to written, formal style: a gradual change seen in progress, good or bad: 景気は回復しつつある 'the economy is recovering'. With change verbs, ている often means the result (変わっている 'has changed; is odd'), so つつある is the way to say 'is in the middle of changing'.
patterns: [change verb dictionary form] ばかりだ

examples.jp: 物価[ぶっか]は上[あ]がる{一方[いっぽう]です}。
examples.en: Prices just keep going up.

examples.jp: 町[まち]の人口[じんこう]は減[へ]る{一方[いっぽう]だ}。
examples.en: The town's population keeps falling.

examples.jp: 父[ちち]の病気[びょうき]は悪[わる]くなる{ばかりだ}。
examples.en: My father's illness only gets worse.

examples.jp: 景気[けいき]は少[すこ]しずつ回復[かいふく]し{つつある}。
examples.en: The economy is gradually recovering.

examples.jp: この村[むら]の生活[せいかつ]も変[か]わり{つつあります}。
examples.en: Life in this village is changing too.

contrast.note: With change verbs ている usually reports the result; つつある shows the change still happening.
た-form + ばかりだ means 'have just done': 着いたばかりだ 'I've just arrived'. Dictionary form + ばかりだ is the worsening trend.
Without ある, stem + つつ means 'while' or 'although': 悪いと知りつつ 'knowing full well it is wrong'.

mistakes.bad: 今[いま]、晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べ{つつある}。
mistakes.good: 今[いま]、晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べ{ている}。
mistakes.note: つつある is for a gradual change, not an ongoing activity.

mistakes.bad: 物価[ぶっか]が{上[あ]がり一方[いっぽう]だ}。
mistakes.good: 物価[ぶっか]が{上[あ]がる一方[いっぽう]だ}。
mistakes.note: 一方だ takes the dictionary form; it is つつある that takes the stem.

skills.tip: Is it a change? Getting steadily worse: ばかりだ. Unstoppable trend: 一方だ. In progress, formal: つつある.

skills.rule: ざるを得ない = circumstances leave me no choice; ないわけにはいかない = duty or decency won't let me not do it; ずにはいられない = I can't hold back the urge.
skills.explain:
All three mean 'I have to', so choose by where the pressure comes from.

ざるを得ない (えない): outside facts force a decision you would rather avoid. ない-stem + ざる: 行かざるを得ない. する becomes せざるを得ない. Formal: 雨がひどいので中止せざるを得ない.

ないわけにはいかない: a social or moral reason; not doing it would be wrong or unthinkable. Plain ない-form + わけにはいかない: 友達の結婚式だから出席しないわけにはいかない. Without the ない, dictionary form + わけにはいかない means the opposite: 'I can't (allow myself to) do it'.

ずにはいられない: the pressure is inside you, an emotion or impulse you cannot suppress: 笑わずにはいられない 'can't help laughing', 心配せずにはいられない. ない-stem + ず, with する becoming せず. It is for feelings and spontaneous reactions, not for decisions.
patterns: [ない-stem] ざるを得ない (する → せざるを得ない)
[ない-form] わけにはいかない
[ない-stem] ずにはいられない (する → せずには)

examples.jp: 雨[あめ]がひどいので、試合[しあい]は中止[ちゅうし]{せざるを得[え]ない}。
examples.en: The rain is so bad that we have no choice but to cancel the match.

examples.jp: 社長[しゃちょう]の命令[めいれい]なら、行[い]か{ざるを得[え]ません}。
examples.en: If it's the president's order, I have no choice but to go.

examples.jp: 友達[ともだち]の結婚式[けっこんしき]だから、出席[しゅっせき]し{ないわけにはいかない}。
examples.en: It's my friend's wedding, so I can't not go.

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は大事[だいじ]な試験[しけん]だから、勉強[べんきょう]し{ないわけにはいかない}。
examples.en: I have an important exam tomorrow, so I can't skip studying.

examples.jp: この映画[えいが]を見[み]ると、泣[な]か{ずにはいられない}。
examples.en: I can't help crying whenever I watch this film.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]の話[はなし]を聞[き]いて、笑[わら]わ{ずにはいられなかった}。
examples.en: When I heard his story, I couldn't help laughing.

contrast.note: An inner urge (laughing, crying, worrying), not a reluctant decision forced by facts.
Dictionary form + わけにはいかない means 'can't do it': 行くわけにはいかない 'I can't go'. 'Must go' needs 行かないわけにはいかない.
The neutral 'must'; it does not say where the pressure comes from.

mistakes.bad: 試合[しあい]は中止[ちゅうし]{しざるを得[え]ない}。
mistakes.good: 試合[しあい]は中止[ちゅうし]{せざるを得[え]ない}。
mistakes.note: する becomes せ before ざる and before ず.

mistakes.bad: 熱[ねつ]が高[たか]いので、会社[かいしゃ]を休[やす]ま{ずにはいられない}。
mistakes.good: 熱[ねつ]が高[たか]いので、会社[かいしゃ]を休[やす]ま{ざるを得[え]ない}。
mistakes.note: A fever forces the decision from outside; ずにはいられない is for an urge you can't suppress.

mistakes.bad: 行[い]くと約束[やくそく]したから、{行[い]くわけにはいかない}。
mistakes.good: 行[い]くと約束[やくそく]したから、{行[い]かないわけにはいかない}。
mistakes.note: To mean 'I must go', keep the ない; without it the sentence says 'I can't go'.

skills.tip: Who is pushing? The situation: ざるを得ない. Duty or other people: ないわけにはいかない. My own feelings: ずにはいられない.

skills.rule: Stem + かねない = something bad could well happen; かねる = I cannot (polite refusal); 得る = it is possible; がたい = hard to bring yourself to, almost impossible.
skills.explain:
All four follow the verb stem.

かねない warns of a risk: 事故になりかねない 'could lead to an accident'. Despite the negative ending it means 'may', and only for bad outcomes.

かねる is the mirror image: despite the positive ending it means 'cannot', and it is the polite way staff refuse: お答えしかねます 'I'm afraid I can't answer'. It implies you would like to, but your position does not allow it.

得る says something is possible in principle: 起こり得る 'could happen'. The dictionary form is read うる or える (あり得る is usually ありうる); the other forms use え: 得ない (えない), 得ます (えます). あり得ない means 'impossible, unthinkable'. It is about possibility, not personal ability, which is the potential form.

がたい means your mind or feelings resist the act: 信じがたい 'hard to believe', 許しがたい 'unforgivable', 理解しがたい. For physical or practical difficulty use にくい: この字は読みにくい.
patterns: [verb stem] 得る (うる / える) / 得ない (えない)

examples.jp: そんなことは、あり{得[え]ない}。
examples.en: That's impossible.

examples.jp: 地震[じしん]はいつでも起[お]こり{得[う]る}。
examples.en: An earthquake can happen at any time.

examples.jp: そんな運転[うんてん]をしたら、事故[じこ]になり{かねない}。
examples.en: Driving like that could easily cause an accident.

examples.jp: その件[けん]については、お答[こた]えし{かねます}。
examples.en: I'm afraid I'm unable to comment on that matter.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]が嘘[うそ]をついたなんて、信[しん]じ{がたい}。
examples.en: It's hard to believe that he lied.

contrast.note: かねない (negative form) = 'may well happen'; かねる (positive form) = 'cannot'. The forms point the opposite way to the meaning.
にくい is practical difficulty (読みにくい字 'hard-to-read writing'); がたい is psychological resistance (信じがたい).
Neutral 'might', good or bad; かねない only for a feared result.

mistakes.bad: この薬[くすり]を飲[の]めば、すぐ治[なお]り{かねない}。
mistakes.good: この薬[くすり]を飲[の]めば、すぐ治[なお]る{かもしれない}。
mistakes.note: かねない is only for bad outcomes; a hoped-for recovery takes かもしれない.

mistakes.bad: このペンは書[か]き{がたい}。
mistakes.good: このペンは書[か]き{にくい}。
mistakes.note: A pen that is awkward to use is a practical difficulty: にくい. がたい is for what your mind won't accept.

skills.tip: Feared risk: かねない. Polite 'I can't': かねる. Possible: 得る. Mind resists: がたい.
